name: Facial Autologous Muscular Injection (FAMI)

lead: FAMI is a facial fat-grafting approach in which a person's own fat is injected into facial muscle to restore volume and contour, giving a fuller, more contoured face. A 2007 review lists it with lipostructure and facial fat rebalancing as newer concepts for three-dimensional rejuvenation of the whole face.

Fat is harvested from elsewhere on the body and injected into facial muscle, as the name describes. Little else is published on it specifically, and the same review notes that practical ways to measure fat-transfer outcomes objectively are lacking.

paras: It is a clinic procedure done by a surgeon, with fat taken from one area of the body and placed in the face. Swelling settles over days to weeks, and part of the fat may be reabsorbed before the final result.
General fat-grafting references list swelling, bruising, haematoma, contour irregularities, infection and partial reabsorption of the fat. FAMI-specific safety data were not found.

chain: Own fat injected into facial muscle
angle.text: The payoff is restored volume and a fuller, more contoured face using the patient's own fat. Fat is harvested and injected into facial muscle. A 2007 review lists it among newer fat-transfer concepts, and little is published on it specifically.

lead: Facial Autologous Muscular Injection (FAMI), also written as fat autograft muscle injection, is a facial fat-grafting technique in which the patient's own fat is injected into facial muscle for volume restoration and contouring. A 2007 review of fat transfer lists it with lipostructure and facial fat rebalancing as newer concepts aimed at three-dimensional rejuvenation of the whole face [1].

The same review states that practical means of objectively measuring fat-transfer outcomes are lacking [1]. Wikipedia mentions FAMI only in a notice proposing to merge a separate FAMI article into its fat grafting article, and does not describe the technique [2]. Evidence specific to FAMI is very limited.
infobox: Autologous fat grafting into facial muscle

paras: A 2007 review describes fat augmentation as safe, relatively inexpensive and readily available, and says surgeons increasingly recognise that facial aging reflects atrophy of tissue as well as gravity, which has made fat use for volume restoration more popular [1]. General references describe fat grafting for the mouth and eye regions and list swelling, bruising, haematoma, contour irregularity, infection and injury to underlying structures as complications, with some of the transferred fat reabsorbed over time [2].
No studies found. The 2007 review discusses FAMI among varying concepts of fat transfer but the available abstract does not report outcome data for it [1].
